e-9179.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
e-9179.problem:
The table below describes how the customers of a particular electronics store feel about their next computer purchase.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Laptop** | **Desktop** |
| To: | **Laptop** | $0.9$ | $0.8$ |
| **Desktop** | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |  |

It is found that $10 \%$ of customers who currently use a laptop would choose a desktop on their next purchase, while $80 \%$ of customers who currently use a desktop would choose a laptop on their next purchase. 

Given that the store has $5\,400$ customers, all of whom purchase a new computer every two years, how many customers would eventually own a desktop computer if the given probabilities remain constant over many two-year periods?
e-9179.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/1935c4960a48e2b446c2610b9edc2a160a5f45462494c72a90f139ea2d13cc34.png)

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many two-year periods, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/29b5a209bb27b24f165ee418326763d8fb24f83f2b3a767052c381aa8cd0e01c.png)

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=8{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/0e8f620c3392dbb77b1353184e38eaf48b526aa82c502772a5582bd20c7f5aea.png)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 9{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our steady-state vector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/2ed7b0fc7296b2b651909c7c15c73e253fc8a9f95fb037072228d5de6f838894.png)

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{9}}}$ of the $5\,400$ customers would eventually own a desktop computer. Therefore, the total number of people who would eventually own a desktop computer is

$$
\dfrac{1}{9} \cdot 5\,400 = 600.
$$

e-9180.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix
e-9180.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/093de94431946cb83e7cc0523405989b7a23cc8d9677bdecdfba7aaf207fd62b.png)

Find the steady-state vector $\mathbf q$ of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above.
e-9180.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/5ed2f76d9b2857134a5b2aa5781711f9625cabb46a9ca3c3d54aa31c32bb4dbe.png)

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.3 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.7 & 0.4 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=20{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=20{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-18 & 6 & 10 & 0 \\ 2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 14 & 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ -18 & 6 & 10 & 0 \\ 14 & 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-7{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -57 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 57 & -19 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -57 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2x_1 -7\left(\dfrac{1}{3}x_3\right) + x_3 = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}x_3.
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/9ae5533dc825d2d3d08ca7a54c50578e21dda8fad7988b9043baaad2a69368b7.png)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14061943/assets/fd7775b5d982d0bc51e80417a70b67dbff0176afcc5ff9aec613947076201386.png)

after.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{18}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \\ \frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{13}{18}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is

$$

From:
Car Train
To: Car 0.35 0.25
Train 0.65 0.75

It's found that 65% of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while 25% of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year.

Assuming that the town has 90000 people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?

a
60000
b
62000
c
65000
d
63000
e
64000
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix P=[0.350.250.650.75].

Notice that P contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.350.250.650.75]−[1001]=[−0.650.250.65−0.25].

So, the matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.650.2500.65−0.250]R2:=R2+R1∼[−0.650.250000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=513x2.

Hence, the general solution is [513x2x2],x2∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have 513x2+x2=11813x2=1x2=1318.

Therefore, q=[5181318].

So, 1318 of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is 1318⋅90000=65000.

content.problem:
There are two groups of people In a small town: those who travel to work by car and those who travel by train. Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Car** | **Train** |
| To: | **Car** | $0.35$ | $0.25$ |
| **Train** | $0.65$ | $0.75$ |  |

It's found that $65%$ of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while $25%$ of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year.

Assuming that the town has $90\,000$ people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?
content.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{18}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \\ \frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{13}{18}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is

$$
\frac{13}{18}\cdot 90\,000=65\,000.
$$

content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & -0.1\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{6}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{1}{7}-\frac{6}{7}=-\frac{5}{7}.$

$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.75{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 75{x}_{1}-60{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9} \\ \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 1 \\ 0.65 & 0\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 1 \\ 0.65 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 1 \\ 0.65 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.65{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 65{x}_{1}-100{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 13{x}_{1}-20{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{20}{13}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{20}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{20}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{33}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{33}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{20}{33} \\ \frac{13}{33}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{20}{33}-\frac{13}{33}=\frac{7}{33}.$

after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.1\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & -0.8 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.9\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.6 & 0.9 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 & 9 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -12 & 18 & 0 \\ 0 & 12 & -18 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -12 & 18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-6{x}_{1}+6(\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3})+9{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{11}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{11} \\ \frac{3}{11} \\ \frac{2}{11}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{6}{11}+\frac{3}{11}-\frac{2}{11}=\frac{7}{11}.

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.1\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]

content.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & -0.8 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.9\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.6 & 0.9 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 & 9 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -12 & 18 & 0 \\ 0 & 12 & -18 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -12 & 18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-6{x}_{1}+6(\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3})+9{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{11}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{11} \\ \frac{3}{11} \\ \frac{2}{11}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{6}{11}+\frac{3}{11}-\frac{2}{11}=\frac{7}{11}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{aligned}].

$$

after.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 3 & -8 & 6.5 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -7.5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}+0.5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$
